"ABSTRACT:
The conventional direct position determination (DPD) algorithms impose significant communication overhead since the raw signals are required to be transmitted from all sensor stations to a central processor. To address this challenge, we propose a communication-efficient approach for multisource localization, named OBSBL-DPD, which integrates 1-bit quantized measurements with sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). The utilization of 1-bit quantization reduces the communication load between the central processor and distributed stations, while SBL improves the localization accuracy by exploiting signal sparsity. In contrast to existing \ell _1 -penalty-based DPD approaches, the proposed framework employs SBL to solve the localization problems with partially unknown dictionaries in a sparsity-driven way. Moreover, the traditional single-snapshot model is extended to support multi-snapshot scenarios, which can further enhance robustness in practical applications. Additionally, we introduce an alternating minimization strategy to improve the convergence of the proposed algorithm. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed OBSBL-DPD method exhibits superior localization accuracy and reduced computational complexity compared to conventional DPD approaches.

To address this challenge, we propose a communication-efficient approach for multisource localization, named OBSBL-DPD, which integrates 1-bit quantized measurements with sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). The utilization of 1-bit quantization reduces the communication load between the central processor and distributed stations, while SBL improves the localization accuracy by exploiting signal sparsity. In contrast to existing l1-penalty-based DPD approaches, the proposed framework employs SBL to solve the localization problems with partially unknown dictionaries in a sparsity-driven way. Moreover, the traditional single-snapshot model is extended to support multi-snapshot scenarios, which can further enhance robustness in practical applications. Additionally, we introduce an alternating minimization strategy to improve the convergence of the proposed algorithm. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed OBSBL-DPD method exhibits superior localization accuracy and reduced computational complexity compared to conventional DPD approaches. Index Terms—1-bit quantization, alternating minimization strategy, direct position determination (DPD), sparse Bayesian learning (SBL), sparsity-based localization model. I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED WORK W IRELESS localization technologies have attracted extensive research interest due to their critical role in a wide range of applications [1]. In civilian applications, localization systems are widely utilized in cellular networks, environment monitoring, and navigation [3]. Moreover, the rapid advancement of intelligent transportation systems has further emphasized the importance of high-accuracy localization for the effective management and maintenance of transportation infrastructure [4]. Localization systems typically adopt a two-step subsequential estimation process [5]. In the first stage, intermediate parameters such as time difference of arrival (TDOA), direction of arrival (DOA), and frequency difference of arrival (FDOA) are estimated [6], [7]. These parameters are then used in the second stage to determine the positions of the sources [8]. The two-step approach offers several advantages in previous studies. By decoupling parameter estimation from position calculation, it significantly reduces the computational complexity, especially in scenarios involving multiple sources or large-scale sensor networks [9]. Moreover, since each receiving station can estimate the intermediate parameters independently, the need for centralized data fusion is minimized, which reduces the communication load and enhances scalability. 1558-1748 © 2025 IEEE. Since the intermediate parameters are estimated independently at each receiving station, the method fails to fully exploit the fact that all received signals originate from the same emitter [10]. Furthermore, the remaining signal data are typically discarded after extracting these useful parameters, which may result in the loss of weak but informative components embedded in noise [11]. In multisource scenarios, an additional data association step is required, leading to increased system complexity and computational cost. In contrast to the traditional two-step approach, Weiss [12] introduced an alternative method known as direct position determination (DPD). DPD is a single-step technique that directly utilizes the raw data collected from all stations jointly, thereby eliminating the intermediate parameter estimation process [13]. Specifically, it estimates the source position by maximizing a cost function established by all the raw signals. DPD demonstrates superior performance over the two-step methods by avoiding the information loss associated with parameter extraction, particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scenarios [14]. Furthermore, DPD exhibits enhanced robustness, as it inherently mitigates the need for data association by directly operating on the raw measurements. A variety of DPD algorithms have been proposed in recent years. Among these, the most representative approaches include multiple signal classification (MUSIC) [15], maximum likelihood (ML) [16], and minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) [17]. However, each of these approaches has inherent limitations. The MUSIC-based approaches require the prior knowledge of source number, while the ML-based methods are often computationally intensive in multisource scenarios, and the performance of MVDR-based algorithms could be degraded in the presence of coherent sources or array imperfections [18]. These challenges highlight the need for more robust and computationally efficient DPD frameworks. Sparse signal processing and compressed sensing (CS) have attracted considerable attention over the past decade, particularly in the field of source localization [19], [20]. By exploiting the signal sparsity in an appropriate domain, CS enables the reconstruction of high-dimensional parameters from limited measurements via l1-norm optimization, thereby overcoming the limitations imposed by the Nyquist sampling criterion. As for DPD, CS-based methods address several fundamental challenges by enabling sparse signal reconstruction under low SNR conditions and supporting localization in underdetermined scenarios through compressed measurements. Recent studies have further explored the integration of adaptive sparsity models and deep learning techniques to enhance reconstruction accuracy and scalability, making CS-based DPD as a promising direction for next-generation localization systems. A. Application of SBL in Parameter Estimation The methods based on CS are typically classified into three categories. The first includes greedy algorithms [21], [22], which iteratively match the observed signals with atoms in the sensing matrix. These methods are computationally efficient but often rely on accurate prior knowledge of the sparse vector’s structure. The second category consists of convex optimization-based approaches that reformulate sparse recovery as a norm-constrained optimization problem, including methods such as basis pursuit (BP) [23], BP denoising (BPDN) [24], and Lasso [25]. Although these methods typically offer superior performance, their solutions may not always converge to the global optimum. The third category is Bayesian compressive sensing, with sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) being the most representative approach [26]. The approach based on SBL estimates sparse vectors by iteratively approximating the maximum a posteriori (MAP) solution without requiring detailed prior knowledge. Compared to methods such as BP, SBL has demonstrated superior performance in various signal recovery scenarios [27]. By establishing a sparse model for array signal processing, sparse reconstruction algorithms can be applied to recover the received signals and enable accurate parameter estimation. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional DPD methods by reducing the number of sampling snapshots as well as the costs of data transmission, storage, and processing. A comparison with the classical DPD algorithm in [28] shows that the SBL-based method performs more accurately under low SNR conditions. Moreover, it operates effectively without requiring prior knowledge of the number of sources, and it also remains robust even when only a few snapshots are available. Furthermore, the work in [29] indicates that the SBL-based DPD algorithm maintains its superior performance even in the presence of mutual coupling effects between array elements. In [30], a multiple-sparse Bayesian learning (MSBL) algorithm was proposed for channel estimation in broadband millimeter-wave multiple-input–multiple-output (MIMO) orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. The simulation results in [30] show that the algorithm can accurately estimate the beamspace channels and outperforms traditional methods in normalized mean square error (NMSE). Many algorithms for parameter estimation, such as block SBL (BSBL), MSBL [31], and inverse-free SBL (IFSBL) [32], have been proposed and discussed in [33]. The SBL-based framework not only exhibits superior performance but also addresses the signal reconstruction challenges in highly correlated sources and limited snapshots scenarios. B. Application of 1-bit Quantization in DPD While the SBL-based DPD algorithm offers notable advantages, it suffers from high computational complexity, which limits its practicality in real-time or resource-constrained scenarios. In general, DPD algorithms require centralized processing of raw signals transmitted from distributed sensing nodes. Achieving high localization accuracy in distributed systems typically requires extended signal acquisition times, which substantially increase the demands on data storage and transmission. Furthermore, the deployment of high-resolution analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) raises the requirements in communication bandwidth and power consumption, resulting in exponentially rising costs in distributed systems [34]. These demands are impractical for resource-constrained applications, such as energy-efficient arrays or large-scale sensor systems Authorized licensed use limited to: XIDIAN UNIVERSITY. In such scenarios, the performance of both conventional DPD algorithms and SBL-based techniques is severely limited. To reduce the computational complexity and communication load, recent studies have investigated the use of 1-bit ADCs, which preserve only the sign information of the received signals[36],[37]. In contrast to infinite-resolution ADCs, 1-bit ADCs provide a promising alternative by substantially decreasing the transmission cost and power consumption via minimal bitwidth. Recent works have introduced efficient methods for parameter estimation with 1-bit quantized data, such as DOA determination, frequency estimation, and channel estimation[38],[39]. DPD algorithms based on 1-bit signals have also been developed from various perspectives, as demonstrated in[40],[41]. Zhang et al.[42]derived a cost function from 1-bit signals and directly estimated the source location via the ML method. The work in [43] established an identifiability condition of the 1-bit DPD model, relying only on second-order statistical properties. Furthermore, it demonstrated that the 1-bit DPD method could achieve asymptotic localization performance. In [44], 1-bit ADCs were employed in a distributed array system, and a 1-bit DPD method based on MUSIC (1-bit DPD-MUSIC) was proposed. The 1-bit DPD-MUSIC method provided higher computational efficiency and improved localization accuracy compared to the ML-based 1-bit DPD method. C. Our Approach and Contribution SBL-based methods have shown strong potential in signal processing, offering lower computational complexity along with higher robustness and estimation accuracy [45]. These advantages motivate the exploration of direct localization algorithms within sparse Bayesian frameworks. In this work, we propose a DPD method based on SBL and 1-bit data quantization (OBSBL-DPD) for multisource scenarios. The use of 1-bit data reduces the communication bandwidth required for direct positioning while simultaneously decreasing the computational cost. The main contributions of this article are listed as follows. 1) We propose a 1-bit direct positioning approach that substantially reduces communication bandwidth requirements during signal transmission. This method effectively lowers computational complexity and is well-suited for broadband signal reconnaissance, resulting in improved efficiency in a centralized processing framework. 2) A DPD model based on SBL is developed to improve the localization accuracy in multisource scenarios. The proposed model simplifies the selection of regularization parameters in classical norm-based methods, enhancing the robustness and reliability of the localization process. 3) An alternating optimization algorithm is introduced to iteratively update the model parameters of SBL, thereby ensuring convergence of the objective function and improving the stability of the solution. The rest of this article is organized as follows. The localization problem is formulated in Section II. Section III introduces the proposed OBSBL-DPD estimator, including its application to single-snapshot cases and its extension to multiple-snapshot scenarios. Numerical results are presented in Section IV. Finally, the conclusion of this article is drawn in Section V. Throughout this article, we use the following symbols. SBL DIRECT LOCALIZATION ALGORITHM BASED ON 1-BIT SIGNAL In this section, we present a detailed derivation of the proposed OBSBL-DPD. For simplicity, we first consider the case of a single temporal sample and then extend the method to multiple samples. The proposed approach consists of the following stages. 1) Sparse Prior Assumption of the Signal: An priori assumption is considered regarding the received data and the signal envelope of the source. In this article, the signal is assumed to follow a Laplacian prior distribution to promote sparsity. 2) Bayesian Parameter Derivation: An iterative update of the hyperparameters is performed using the expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm. NUMERICAL SIMULATION Simulation experiments are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed OBSBL-DPD algorithm. All sources and receivers are located in the xoy plane, with two sources at (−2, 2) km and (−1.2, 0.2) km. We consider L = 5 spatially distributed stations, each equipped with an antenna array of M = 8 elements. The sources transmit band-limited pulses at a carrier frequency of f0 = 1 GHz. At each station, the received signals are quantized by 1-bit ADCs and sampled over 512 snapshots. Computational Complexity In this section, we compare the computational complexity of the proposed method with that of the SBL-DPD algorithm in [47]. The main computational cost of the proposed OBSBL-DPD algorithm is composed of (30) and the inverse process in (31). The adoption of 1-bit quantization enables the replacement of most multiplication-intensive operations with simple additions, thereby reducing computational load. For each iteration, the complexity of (30) is O[GML + G2ML], while (31) requires O[G3 + G2ML + G], yielding a total complexity of O[G3 + G2ML + GML + G]. In contrast, the SBL-DPD algorithm in [47] exhibits a complexity of O[G3 L + G2ML + G2 + G M2 L2 + GML + M3 L3]. The comparison indicates that the proposed method reduces the computational cost by several orders of magnitude. As illustrated in Fig. 10, the proposed algorithm demonstrates less complexity than the SBL-DPD algorithm as the number of sensors increases. Moreover, 1-bit quantization of the received data reduces data link transmission requirements, thereby enhancing the practical applicability of DPD. The use of 1-bit quantization reduces the communication overhead between receiving stations, which provides a more efficient and cost-effective DPD framework. Moreover, the incorporation of the SBL algorithm compensates for quantization-induced information loss with enhanced localization accuracy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed OBSBL-DPD method achieves comparable localization performance to MUSIC-based and MVDR-based DPD algorithms.
